utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then one final matter, Exhibit D1568 of the Law on Criminal Procedure tendered by the Cermak Defence. That is, the whole of the text in B/C/S, we could consider whether it would not be wise to cut that down as well, so that we only have in B/C/S those articles that were translated but at least we have now the complete set the Cermak Defence wished to have in evidence. Having gone through these procedural matters, is the Gotovina Defence ready to call its next witness, which is Mr. -- no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Herrick. And I do understand that in line with the decision of the 6th of July of this year that representatives of the government of the United States of America will be present in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom and could the representatives of the government accompany him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Herrick. I'll come to you in a second. I'd first like the representatives of the government of the United States of America to introduce themselves to the Court. If you could switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honours. May it please the Court. My name is Karen Johnson. I'm with the office of the legal councillor at the US embassy in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Johnson. And you're with?

utterances.speaker: MS. SKIBSURD
utterances.text: I'm Elisa Skibsrud, and I'm with the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Skibsurd. If there is any matter which you'd like to raise, you're invited to address the Court, not the party at that moment examining the witness, not the witness, but the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Herrick, before we you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite to you stand and to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Herrick. Please be seated. Mr. Herrick, you will first be examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, can you state your full name for the record and spell your last name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: My name is Richard Clinton Herrick, H-e-r-r-i-c-k.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel Herrick, do you recall meeting with members of the Gotovina Defence, the team, on two dates, 11 October 2006 and 14 May of 2009?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you recall that you signed a statement on the 2nd of July of 2009?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Court's permission, if we could bring up 65 ter 1D2773. And, Mr. President, we have a hard copy of the statement for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Herrick, before we embark on this, you and I both speak English if we could just pace ourselves, just a bit so the translators can keep up with us. Both of us mindful of that would be helpful. Colonel Herrick, I showed you -- it is a document that's before you, and do you recognise the document that is before you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recognise that as the statement that you signed on 2 July 2009?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review it before you came to court today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, looking at this statement, you mentioned a clarification -- one clarification, point 5. If you turn to page 2 in the first sentence you noted that that should be the Vance Plan and not the Vance-Owen Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the exception of that clarification in paragraph 5, would the statement that's before you accurately reflect what you said to the members of the Gotovina Defence teams on the two occasion us that met with them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And was the information that you provided true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if today, if I asked you the same questions concerning the information that is set forth in your statement, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2773.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that becomes Exhibit D1578.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1578 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I explained to Colonel Herrick the purpose of the summary statement that I will now read with Your Honours' permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Richard Herrick is a retired lieutenant-colonel from the United States army who was the United States military attache to the Republic of Croatia for a three-year tour from August 1993 to 2 August 1995. As the military attache, Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick was responsible for advising the United States ambassador on military affairs and for observing the host's military activities. Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick met General Ante Gotovina approximately 12 times between 1992 and 1995, where they would have in-depth conversations. He found General Gotovina to be very serious about his job, professional in his demeanour, able to run a professional headquarters, and was well respected by his soldiers. Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick was favourably impressed with General Gotovina. Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick performed an initial assessment of the Croatian army, the HV, when he arrived in his post as military attache in August 1992. At that point, the HV was a militia/National Guard army. The HV had some professional soldiers from the JNA, as well as some former French Foreign Legion soldiers who were commissioned officers. Regardless, the HV did not have sufficient qualified officers. Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick witnessed development and improvement of the professional units of the HV after its inception over time until he left Croatia on 2 August 1995. He credits much of this development and improvement to the former French Foreign Legion officers, such as General Gotovina, because they had previously received formal military training and in many cases themselves had been senior non-commissioned officers in the Foreign Legion. Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick is aware of General Gotovina's influence on training, including a training school established by General Gotovina in Zadar, Croatia. He was briefed on the training done at this school, and his recollection is that the school focussed on teaching small-unit combat. During the summer of 1994, Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick attended a training exercise on the island of Vir, in Croatia. The exercise was conducted by a unit of the 4th Guards Brigade of the HV under the command of General Gotovina. His impression was that it was executed very well and professionally done. While the HV still needed additional training on many levels, it was at this point that Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick became convinced that the HV had the ability to fight as a brigade. One issue the HV faced was the lack of qualified non-commissioned officers which are the backbone of any army. While Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick started to see an improvement in the NCOs in the HV professional brigades over time due to training programmes, the HV's Home Guard units always had problems of poor NCOs. Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick had discussions with General Gotovina about training and educating his troops to comply with the Law of Armed Conflict and proper treatment of civilians. In 1993, General Gotovina informed him that all of his subordinate commanders were already ordered to train their soldiers to follow the Law of Armed Conflict, to treat civilians properly and to avoid atrocities. With respect to Operation Flash in early May 1995, Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick notes that the objective was to open the highway across central Croatia. In the process, the HV captured Sector West. The operation was well organised and well conducted. Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick never received the impression that the objective was to drive the Serbs out of Sector West. According to Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick, the general assessment of the international community prior to Operation Storm was that if the HV attacked the ARSK, they would lose. Did he not share this view. He assessed that the ARSK was stretched too far along the lines of defence and they had no defence in depth. Together with support from its artillery, he surmised that the HV could mass their forces at a certain point along the line, break through at that point, end up behind the ARSK lines quickly, and the fight would be over within two to three days. Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick would interface with Krajina Serbs when he would visit the Krajina with the United States Ambassador Peter Galbraith. With respect to negotiations prior to Operation Storm, Serbs would agree to negotiate but it was just a delay tactic and they were not interested in peaceful reintegration. Prior to Operation Storm, Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick had a conversation with Markica Rebic about the attack and what the response of the international community would be. He told Mr. Rebic that while he could not speak for the international community, he believed that if the operation was done quickly and civilians were safeguarded as was done in May 1995 during Operation Flash, there would be little or no issues with the international community. While Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick departed Croatia on 2 August 1995, he was able to discuss Operation Storm as he was informed in a general sense of the upcoming operation prior to his departure. He was not surprised about the use of the artillery during the operation. Any military planner would use artillery in this situation. Operation Storm was an almost classic classroom example of an offensive military operation from a tactical standpoint. Lieutenant-Colonel Herrick does not believe that the operation was designed to drive the Serbs out of the Krajina. Operation Storm was designed to re-take Croatian territory. That is basically the statement of Colonel Herrick, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, as we discussed previously I'm just going to discuss several items in -- that are set out in the course of your statement and certainly not all of it. And the first -- the first item I'd like to talk to you about is in paragraph 4 of your statement where you talk about the in-depth conversations that had you with General Gotovina approximately 12 times between 1992 and 1995. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And can you tell us about those discussions, Colonel Herrick, the topics that were discussed and where those discussions took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Part of my mission from the United States government in coordination with the [indiscernible] of military attaches was to get an understanding of the military situation in Croatia. I spoke to the defence minister, Mr. Gojko Susak, and got his permission to speak with his senior military leaders. The Krajina in particular, because of the location of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Herrick.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would not mind, I would like to interrupt you. That was a rather simple question. Topics which were discussed and you explained to us that you got the approval to speak with military leaders. If Mr. Kehoe would be interested in knowing there was any issue of approval, or not he will certainly ask you. Could you focus your answer on the question that was put to you which was the topics that were discussed and where those discussions took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we try to use time as efficiently as possible. And again if any further details or any other aspects, if the parties are interested in it, we do not know yet, they will ask you for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The topics dealt with the deployment of Croatian forces, their training, their equipment and their morale. We spoke in his headquarters in Zadar, at restaurants in Zadar, and on occasion at the training centre and in some field locations where he was explaining the training that was going on and I observed some of the training, and then I met him again in -- in Bosnia on the Dinar mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, if question stay with the topics on his deployment of troops. When you met him, did he tell you where his troops were and what the HV was planning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: On the first meeting he took me into his operations centre and showed me his operation map which showed the deployment of his force. He outlined his area of responsibility, but he did not, at that time, tell me what his future plans were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, you also mentioned you discussed training with General Gotovina. Can you give the Trial Chamber a sense of the discussions that you had with General Gotovina about the content of those discussions regarding training and what impressions you took away from those discussions with General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: The discussions started in the very general sense and the fact that the most important thing a commander can do for his soldiers is to properly train them. And he spoke to me about his policy of that. I commented that along with the military arts that soldiers are trained that there are responsibilities of commanders to ensure that their soldiers know the laws of land warfare and the proper conduct of the treatment of prisoners of war and the safety and security of civilians. He expressed that he received training in a prior military, training with the French army, and that he was very cautious of that responsibility and was taking steps or had taken steps to ensure that his commanders were aware of it and the soldiers in the field were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And two time-frames, if you can, Colonel, the discussion that you just talked about where General Gotovina told you that he had received this training in the French army and had taken steps to ensure that his commanders were aware of it, approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That was in the spring of 1993 on the first occasion that I met General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One more time-frame before we go into a couple of more paragraphs in your statement and that is the meeting that you had with General Gotovina on the Dinara. Approximately when that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That was in late spring 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And for what purposes did you go up to the Dinara in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: There were two reasons. One was I had travelled with secretary or Minister Gotovina [sic] into the Livno in December of 1994 and observed the Croatian army/Bosnia army offensive in the Livno valley, and I wanted to get an update on how far that operation had advanced. And the other was that there were allegations against the Croatian forces in Bosnia of firing on United Nations post in the valley below the Dinara, and -- so I got permission from the Ministry of Defence to travel there and observe for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, I believe there is one correction if Your Honour on page 22 on page 2, it talks about a minister -- I take that back, I do believe. When you went to the Dinara in 1995, the minister that you were referring to was whom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: It was Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's clear now. One last question before we go into the training. You commented about the responsibility to train soldiers and that was an important issue. Was that something that was said by you or by General Gotovina or what was the interplay there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I apologise, I can't be more precise, because that conversation was some time ago, but it was a mutually agreed upon discussion that the training was important. I raised it. He concurred and elaborated on what he was do to go train his force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about that before we go back. Let's take it from a macro level before we take it down to the Split Military District level. And I would like to address you, generally, to your paragraphs 6 through 13 where you discuss the development and the training of the HV in Croatia during the time you were there. And without repeating everything there, can you take us through your analysis, Colonel, from your initial assessment and how you observed the training in the HV progressed during your time-frame?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Prior going to my post in Zagreb, I was the US army attache in Belgrade Yugoslavia, and before the United States formally recognised Croatia as a separate country, and I was under US guidance I was still accredited to all the republics of the former Yugoslavia and travelled to each one of those. So I observed JNA forces in the field on their side of the military lines, and on other occasions I would travel to Croatia and observe Croatian forces in the field. This was -- would have been in the summer and fall of 1991 and then in the spring -- winter and spring of 1992. And I saw -- I would characterise as a trained but not particularly effective organised Croatian army in those early days of people who might have had some former military training but did not appear to be well disciplined and organised as an effective fighting force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. If we can just get some definitions if we can because you used the word discipline in the course of your statement, and for the Trial Chamber's purpose, can you describe when you say discipline what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Obviously there's personal discipline and there's military organisational discipline. I'm referring to the later, more specifically here, and you can observe that in field units by the way they're deployed, by the way a unit will be marching along a road and get off the road and take a break. A disciplined unit will do it with a sense of putting out security and being aware of their surroundings but allowing part of the unit to relax while the other part stays attentive to potential combat operations. The times that I observed the Croatian army in the early days, when they took a break, everybody took a break. There was not a sense of impending peril, although in some cases where I was they were not far from potential enemy contact and they otherwise should have been, so it is in that respect that I made that judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the development of this training that you saw in 1992, did you see how the HV began to develop from the smaller unit level to the higher up to the brigade level and can you give us a sense of your observation there and what success that they achieved, if any.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And if I may, I will say I had conversations about this with both Defence Minister Susak and with General Bobetko. And I expressed my observations, and they expressed that they had observed the same things. And General Bobetko had told me that because of that they were -- they were setting up formal training programmes and they were starting with primarily company grade officers and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you talk about a company and you go into this, can you give us an approximate size of soldiers in company, battalion, brigade, et cetera, as you're discussing this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Generally an army company, an infantry company, will consist of somewhere between 100 and 150 soldiers. You would have three to four companies in a battalion. A company might be led by a senior lieutenant or a captain. A battalion would be commanded by, generally, a lieutenant-colonel. And so in order to fight effectively, then you have to all your subordinate commanders and officers and NCOs accordingly trained and that's what both Minister Susak and General Bobetko were concerned about, and that's what I was observing in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about that. Tell us what you were observing in the field and tell us, before we go into specifics, about what you observed. What did you in your conversations with Bobetko and Susak discuss as to what the problem was, especially with regard to NCOs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, most of the Croatian soldiers were either coming out of the police force or the Territorial Defence force of the reserve army of the JNA, and they had been essentially trained as the Territorial Defence force any ways, in basic infantry combat tactics of use of a weapon and the defence of their home town. If attacked, then they were trying to fall back into the hills and conduct delaying tactics and impede the advance of the enemy until the formal army could take action. And so those soldiers were not particularly trained well enough to -- to be an a professional army in my terms or my sense of a NATO force would be. And so they were -- they knew how to use weapons but they did not or nor did they particularly demonstrate good military manoeuvre or the ability to operate as a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us address ourselves directly first to -- to paragraph 7 the last line in your statement where you say: "Because the HV lacked experienced NCOs with years of training, the NCOs that the HV did have were not able to properly instill discipline in the troops." Turning your attention ahead to paragraph 11, where you discuss this further, you note that: "NCOs are the backbone of any army. Ideally an army will have one NCO to supervise eight to ten soldiers, while one officer for 50 to 100 soldiers. As I discussed in paragraph 7, the problem an army faces without adequate number of NCOs is that it results in a fighting force without leaders on the ground potentially resulting in a lack of discipline with armed soldiers responding to the situations viscerally rather than professionally." Colonel, if you could, could you just elaborate a bit on the importance of the NCOs and leading to this final statement that you make about soldiers that don't have adequate -- soldiers responding viscerally rather than professionally because of inadequate NCOs leading them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: If I may, I mention the size of a company. A company is generally made up three platoons. It would be each -- or four platoons and each platoon would be led by a senior NCO, a non-commissioned officer, who is responsible for ensuring that the soldiers continue their military training after they have been to a basic training course, where they would learn how to March in a straight line, shoot a weapon properly, learn how to do a proper field sanitation technique, so they can still stay operational in the field. But after basic training you have to ensure that then individuals who now know the basic skills can operate as a military organisation. And within a platoon, you would have squads and each squad would have a NCO, a junior NCO, and they would be responsible for a team of -- of eight to 12 soldiers, and they would be -- you might have a machine-gun unit and -- where the gunner might now how to fire the machine-gun and he needed to how the unit trains to operate in the field because you certainly wouldn't want your machine-gunner to lay down a field of fire and hit his own soldiers, and you want to make sure that the other infantry soldiers know how the machine-gunner is going it operate so that they don't walk into their own field of fire. Without properly trained NCOs that -- that machine-gun crew, that squad, and that platoon will not effectively operate together and be effective on the field of combat. And in that platoon of 30 soldiers you could have a -- probably a lieutenant who would be organising the platoon activities with -- to coordinate those with the company but it's that platoon Sergeant that is going to make the platoon enlisted men operate as an effective fighting force. And that's why non-commissioned officers are so critical to any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we talked to you a little bit in your statement about training and here today, and again in paragraph 11, you talk about the time commitments necessary to train NCOs to take over be it a squad or platoon. Can you talk to us a little bit about that and I understand the frame of reference is the -- your's is the United States of America, but just generally based on your military experience with the United States and other NATO countries what is the general consensus about what kind of time is necessary for that type of training to have a NCO who is ready to take on that task?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Generally, a junior NCO that would lead a squad of eight to ten people would have three to five years of military experience, both formal training and experience operating in the unit that he is assigned to. A platoon sergeant would probably have eight to ten year, maybe even up to 15 years of experience, and so that there aren't many events that a platoon would be engaged in that he would not have had the experience within that ten-year experience, so he would be able to pass on that training to his junior enlisted men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now what is -- sorry. Now, with regard to military discipline, what is the importance of properly trained non-commissioned officers in the maintenance of military discipline itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, when normally when somebody gets shot at, they will look for cover and for protection. If a military unit comes under fire, if everybody seeks protection, then no one is fighting back, generally. And they become ineffective on the battlefield and so what you have to train a military unit to do is to advance and fire back if you're on the attack, if you're on the defence, then you probably would be fighting from protected positions. It could be a fox hole or it could be a -- if you had time to prepare a position, you would have sand bags and bunkers in order to protect yourself from small-arms and artillery fire. But you do have to train to act, to move forward, and fight in combat and not be concerned about your individual protection. If you do that, then -- if everybody in the unit is only concerned about their individual protection, the unit will probably be destroyed on the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how -- and how does that explanation you just gave us play into your comment about ensuring that -- that soldiers react professionally as opposed to viscerally, just in paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, yeah. My reference was to -- if you're acting individually and you are responding to your immediate emotions, you will be ineffective as a unit, people will not lay down a base of fire in the same direction, on the same or direct the target, and there is certainly no professionalism in that manner of contact. If you are trained to fight as a unit, you understand how you fire and manoeuvre, and part of the unit will lay down protective fire while the other moves forward in combat. The unit that is now in front will put down protective fire and the trail unit will move forward. Those units who operate in that manner who have received that type of training and will operate in that way in combat, and what we find and what we say is that you will fight the way you're trained. And though, therefore, you need to have skilled, trained NCOs to ensure that the unit is effective. Now, a part of that is, as you come across that same professionalism is not only how you fire the weapons as a unit but how do you treat prisoners that you take, or how do you treat innocent civilians who happen to be -- in a military area of operation, and so your unit has to be trained how to respond to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's -- if we may, let's delve a little bit more into that and what we're talking about in regard to discipline as opposed to combat discipline against an opposing force with regard to personal discipline and malfeasance by soldiers, tell us about the role of NCOs in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, an army's form, when government form armies, there are international agreements on how they will conduct themselves, and so how an individual treats a prisoner of war or a civilian in combat, it ties back to their professional leadership and so he needs to be trained and instructed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The "he" being who?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: The individual soldier. Needs to be trained and instructed on how to respond so it becomes a -- well, a course of conduct in battle. The US army is very clear, it has a field manual on the Laws of Land Warfare. It's kind of a subset of the Law of Armed Conflict which is a broader law. And this was a topic of discussion I had with Croatian commanders, with the defence minister and the chief of defence, General Bobetko. And it was a topic of discussion I had with General Gotovina on our first meeting, and I mentioned the US army manual, and he asked me for a copy and we provided it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going back on the role of the NCOs and talking about soldiers who possibly are committing crimes, do the NCOs, themselves, need extensive training on how to deal with the situation when you have soldiers who are possibly committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, they do because not everybody responds the same way despite being train the properly, and so the NCO has to be able to step in and take charge and responsibility for the people assigned underneath them, and so if he has a situation where soldiers began to act inappropriately or illegally, the NCO is legally bound to stop them and correct them on the spot and ensure the safety of either prisoners or innocent civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us now translate this back into the HV during the time-frame you were there and taking into consideration the beginning of the HV through your time in 1995. With regard to these NCOs, what hurdles did the HV have to get over during this relatively short period of time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Generally the soldiers that they had, they were trained by the JNA, were generally not active duty JNA soldiers, and the -- General Bobetko told me that he did not or could not rely on the JNA model because the JNA was a cadre army, and this was something that I had known previously, that was made up of officers and senior NCOs, and -- and that was the standing army, and then young men would be conscripted into the army for 12 to 18 months and would not get a full breadth of military training and experience during that time-period, and then they would be return back to the reserves or to the territorial guard. And so they didn't have the full breadth of military training to include the understanding of the Laws of Land Warfare and not so much that what they had received but to the degree where they could impart that training to somebody else, and this was something that the Croatian senior leaders recognised as something that they had to correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, were you aware of efforts by the HV to cure these deficiencies by training internally as well as by training through outside entities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: The Croatian army set up a training school or an academy for junior officers initially and for -- and they drew -- they began to be very critical of the people who had served in the former JNA because that was not the model of the army they wanted to build, and so they started to look for soldiers who had demonstrated courage and leadership in battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, let me just interrupt you. If you can give the Chamber a time-frame for this, it would be helpful. Approximately.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: This would have -- this started to occur in late 1992, shortly after General Bobetko became the chief of the army. Up to that time General Tus, JNA air force officer, was in charge and he was replaced by General Bobetko. And partly, and partly because that -- and so General Bobetko and his staff began setting up training programmes and turning to the corps commanders to ensure that that was continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about training at the NCO level to cure those deficiencies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, actually, they turned principally to General Gotovina and had him set up a school in Zadar for the training of NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when did that begin, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the exact date, but it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, just looking at the beginning -- excuse me. Before I ask you some questions taking up to 1995. Do you know why they selected Gotovina for this training, to do the training in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I think they had a lot of respect for General Gotovina. Defence Minister Susak told me that he thought General Gotovina was his best combat general, and he had demonstrated the ability to train within his own corps, and they wanted him to extend that training to all the professional brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we talk about the professional brigades and the Home Guard units, Colonel, I mean, based on your experience and the years that you talking about for training in NATO forces, do you think that -- believe that the HV had sufficient time to develop the NCOs to a level of proficiency given the time-frame that they had? A high level of proficiency, I should say.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: No, I don't. While the NCO training course itself might be done in three to six months, that's formal training and you also need practical experience to go along with that. Again, most -- the US army and most NATO countries a junior NCO would have three to five years of training. By the time they started the training course, there is was a two-year period before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there a difference there the training that you observed between the professional brigades that General Gotovina was dealing with and the Home Guard unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian leadership realised that they didn't have the resources to train or the time to train the full army, so they concentrated on the professional brigades and the territorial guards or the reserves continued to train in exercises, but -- field exercises but, for the most part, did not have formal classroom training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, prior it your testimony today, Colonel, you talked about Law of Armed Conflict and how to conduct the law -- excuse me, how to conduct combat pursuant to that law, and you noted had you a conversation with General Gotovina about the Law of Armed Conflict and the treatment -- treatment of civilians and prisoners of war. Is that basically the topic of discussion that your referring to in paragraph 12 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if I can direct your attention to the last sentence of paragraph 12, and I'd just like to ask you some follow-up questions on that score. And we're talking about the topic of treatment of civilians and operating. In accordance to the Law of Armed Conflict, you note that: "With respect to this topic, General Gotovina, in 1993, informed me that all his subordinate commanders ... were already ordered to train their soldiers to follow the Law of Armed Conflict to treat civilians properly and to avoid atrocities." And then in paragraph 13 you go through a bit of a discussion there. Can you give us a sense of that discussion of -- with General Gotovina and what you took away from that and how you began to check whether or not or did you begin to check whether or not that story was true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, we had a discussion on -- on the training of the Law of Armed Conflict, the Law of Land Warfare, which was -- is a US army term, the term I used, and the responsibility of officers and NCOs to ensure that the people -- the soldiers are properly trained and conduct themselves accordingly. This was a topic I raised in an article of Croatian military magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you before you continue on. You raised it in "Hrvatski Vojnik," a Croatian soldier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just show you that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's -- if could I bring that up, Mr. President, 1D2777. Mr. President, I did consult with Mr. Russo prior to this, if I can make an ore tenus motion to add it to the 65 ter list as well. I think Mr. Russo informed me he has no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so, therefore I take it that you will tender it and implicitly ask for adding it to the 65 ter list. That's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is this the article that you're referring to, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yeah, it appears to be so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the handsome chap many years ago. We all looked better 14 years ago. I even had hair. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. President, we'll just offer into evidence 1D2777, adding it to the 65 ter list and admitting it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, since we know the position of the Prosecution already.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, this topic of dealing with civilians and conduct themselves properly was obviously something of importance to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: It was. I had agreed to an interview by Croatian military magazine. They had a list of questions which I responded to. They then asked if there was anything else I wanted to add, and I added the piece on the Law of Land Warfare and the responsibility of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me just go back to the conversation with General Gotovina and what did you to, you know, check the veracity as to what he was telling you. A, what he told you and what you did to check the veracity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: As I would go out in the field to observe and visit units, I would ask soldiers if they had received training, and I cite in this one particular case where I was visiting up on Dinara mountain, and the jeep driver who was -- who was taking me to an area of observation with just myself and my deputy in the vehicle, and so there was no Croatian leader to hear the conversation, I asked him if he had received training in the Laws of Land Warfare and if he had observed any military atrocities in his time in the military, and, at that time, I believe he said he been in three years. He said with quite a bit of pride that he had received it, and in all the time that he been in the army, his unit was very proud that they had not committed any atrocities, and this was something his units, under General Gotovina, had been trained and was -- spoke freely about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, you mention that one example. Did you have this discussion or get this impression with dealing with other soldiers as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I did. But in this particular case, he volunteered that his units was proud that they had not conducted any atrocities in the battles that he had been in. Others had not said that. So this particular case stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what did you take away from that conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, this was approximately two years after my first conversation with General Gotovina, and it -- reinforced the -- my belief that what he told me was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: The training of the Laws of Land Warfare to his soldiers. So, here, a corps commander is telling me what he's done, so the most senior person in the corps is telling me, Here's what we with are doing in our army and a very junior soldier who would -- driving the US defence attache is an important job but not as important as the corps commander, that junior enlisted man had gotten the word. That training had gotten down to his level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I'm going to go into this subject at this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us an indication as to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Mr. President, half an hour, 45 minutes at the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break. Mr. Herrick, when I addressed you as Mr. Herrick, we have seen a lot of military and civilian authorities before us: All rank, titles, academics, medical doctors. This Chamber is used to addressing everyone as mister, which is not, in any way, to be understood as a lack of respect for the achievements from those persons, which is usually expressed by their titles and by their ranks. We will have a break and resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, if I could just get one point of clarification. Earlier today on page 22, line 6, I was asking you about the going up to the Dinara, and I said for what purposes did you go to the Dinara in 1995. And answer on 7, there are two reasons, one was, I was travelling with it was Minister Susak into Livno in the summer of 1994. And if I could go to the sentence that begins on line 10: "And the other was that there were allegations that Croatian forces in Bosnia of firing on United Nations posts in the valley below the Dinara and so I got permission from the Ministry of Defence there to observe for myself?" Colonel, do you know the results of that investigation of allegations that the Croatian forces were firing on an UN post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I ever knew the outcome of that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel let's move ahead in your statement to paragraph 14 where you talk about Operation Flash and your discussions with Minister Susak, and you note that in the fifth line of the objective was to open the highway across central Croatia. The objective of Operation Flash, I take it, was to open the highway across central Croatia; do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit. What is this central highway you're talking about. You know, from your experience in the area, what is the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: It was a divided highway. It was a -- I forget the international highway number, but it was a major commercial route that ran the -- the east/west length of Croatia between -- primarily between Zagreb and Belgrade. It provided -- it was a major commercial issue for Croatia, because it connected the east end of Slovenia with the rest of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Had there been discussions with the Krajina Serbs about opening that highway, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: There were, and discussions with Belgrade leadership. And than had been -- the conversation had been going back and forth. At one time it appeared as though the Serbs were going to agree, and at the last minute they changed their mind, and I believe this happened several times and it -- finally a decision was made within the Croatian government to open it by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now were these negotiations prior to Operation Flash consistent with your comment in paragraph 18 that the Krajina Serbs were not interested about agree to go a peaceful reintegration into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: They contributed to that understanding, but I believe what I'm referring to here are negotiations that Ambassador Galbraith was directly involved with, with other ambassadors in Croatia to open a dialogue between Knin and Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just go back, if we may, to paragraph 14 and your discussions with Minister Susak, where you discuss the objective and the fact that the HV took Sector West. Now, did you have discussions with Minister Susak as to -- with respect to the follow-up operations after the military operation in Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: We did, and I had discussions with Ambassador Galbraith as well. We were concerned for the safety of citizens in the region, and we went and made several visits, and I don't recall the names of the towns we went to, but we went to several locations to observe that it was under -- after the incursion that it was under civilian law or civilian rule and that the rights of the citizens in Sector West were being --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now this statement that you have under civilian law, civilian rule, can you explain how that came about and can you explain how you came to your understanding that it was under civilian law and rule?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, the operation, Operation Flash, was characterised to us as a police operation that -- and the police were being supported by the army but that the police were in charge of the operation. When I was notified of the -- that the operation was about to occur, it was about 1.00 or 2.00 in the morning, and our -- the escorts said, We're going to take you to the operations centre. We, in fact, went to the police headquarters and received a briefing. We did not go to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding based on your discussions with Croatian officials as to what the army's role was and how long they were supposed to stay and what they were supposed to do when the operation was complete?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Because there were armed RSK soldiers from the army of the Republika Srpska in the Krajina, the army would deal with those forces but the rest of it would be under police operations and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note in paragraph 14 that the operation was well organised and well conducted. What's the basis of your position on that score? And that's in paragraph 14, the second-to-last sentence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: It was my understanding, for the basis of that comment, was the briefing I received and how the operation would be conducted, that the fact that UN forces in the sector would be notified prior to any military contact, and -- and that their rights to be secured and safety would be secured as well, that the UN forces were notified and UN headquarters was notified, and that the rights of civilians would be ensured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The last sentence on that paragraph that you say: "I never received the impression that the objective was to drive the Serbs out of Sector West." Tell us the basis for that impression, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That was not declared as one of the objectives. And then as I went into Sector West and spoke to Serb citizens and other officers from the US embassy and other embassies went into Sector West, the Croatian government made it possible for foreign government representatives to go and see for themselves, not just it take the word of the Croatian government. And in those discussions with Serb citizens, we felt that their rights were being observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic -- Mr. Kehoe, I missed the beginning of the answer here. If could you look with me on the screen, page 41, line 17, you were asked about the basis for your impression that you never received -- that you never received the impression that the objective was to drive the Serbs out of Sector West. And then you said that was not one of ... I remember that you said something. It was not one of the reasons given to you or is it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was when I received the briefing on the operation, it was not one of the objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then when I went into Sector West and spoke with Serb citizens, the conversations I had with them was that their rights were being protected. They were, of course, fearful but they said they had not been mistreated and had not been -- their rights objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Perhaps if you could just take a little pause between question and answer, and Mr. Kehoe will do the same - I know that - then we'll not have any risk that part of your testimony would be lost.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move out of Sector West, I mean, at this time, Colonel, was the HV large enough to hold ground like that which was in Sector West and also meet other possible military contingencies around Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, it was large enough to accomplish the mission in taking Sector West. It was a very quick operation, and army forces vacated the region as soon the objective was achieved, and police forces were in -- were responsible and I observed that in the locations I went to. I'm not -- I -- I'm not sure what other contingencies you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To the extent that they had to meet other possible combat operations against either the VRS or against the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: No other operations occurred at the time so I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move up to the other operations, if we can, and if we can move back to the Dinara and just go paragraph 16 where you talk about your assessment of the situation prior to Operation Storm and the fact that there was no depth in the defence by the ARSK. Now, prior to Operation Storm, you were -- were you -- you were aware of military operations being conducted by General Gotovina up in the Dinara area in June of 1995, were you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a US code cable, 1D2775, dated 16 June 1995. You have seen this document before today, Colonel, have you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as I said, this is a cable for 16 June 1995. In the summary: "The Croatian army concluded its seizing of key terrain in the Dinara mountains overlooking Knin as of 11 June 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go down to - that's at the bottom of the page - paragraph 22. I'm not quite sure what the numerical sequencing, Mr. President, is. There's a second 2 in the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: These cables are written in three parts, a summary, a text, and a comment section. So you have a text 1 and a text 2, a comment section, 1, 2, and so on. If I were referring to this, I would say in the comments section, paragraph 2. Perhaps that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It notes -- in paragraph 1 there, it notes the taking of that ground on the Dinara of paragraph 2: "HV corps commander Major-General Ante Gotovina commands the operation in the Dinara mountains and has been given orders to stop with the terrain he currently holds and not to conduct any actions which would precipitate a further military response from the Krajina Serbs. The Croatian government does not believe that the ... military [sic] resolution to the crisis is possible and is prepared to move militarily to retake the Serb occupied parts of Croatia." Discussing this particular military operation and General Gotovina being up on the Dinara, is this consistent with what you knew at the time in June, mid-June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 2D2775.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1580.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now this Chamber has -- likewise, as we move from June into July, this Chamber has received quite a bit of evidence about what was going on with regard to the Bihac pocket. And I'd like to show you another cable on that score from July the 24th of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we could bring up 1D2774.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As I noted, this was the cable of 24 July 1995, the summary at the top: "Croatian ... forces prepare to draw Krajina Serb forces away from Bihac to counter the Serb offensive in the UN Safe Area. Bihac is strategically important to Croatia and Croatia is not prepared to let it fall to Serb forces." If we could turn the page, paragraph 3, the last sentence: "This push would include neutralising Serb forces in Titov, Drvar, and Bosanski Petrovac, recognise the extreme risk this entails but asserted that the fall of Bihac entails a greater risk to Croatia." And if you could show you another document in conjunction with this, Colonel, so we can move through this quickly. I would like to bring up 1D2776, a cable dated 28 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just getting a little feedback on this microphone. If I could just switch to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This cable, sir, is 28 July. If we go to the summary first: "The Croatian army and Croatian Defence Council captured the towns of Bosansko Grahovo and Glamoc on 28 July 1995. Portions of the Grahovo Knin and Grahovo Drvar roads are now also under Croatian control. Titov, Drvar is the next operational objective." If we go down to the bottom of the page under 2: "Croatian analysts were surprised at the lack of depth of Serb defences. Serb front lines were well fortified but once forced," we turn the page, "from their front line bunkers, they had no second or third line of defence." Again, these two cables, sir, are these consistent with what you knew about what was going on on the ground just prior to the combat in Bosansko Grahovo and Glamoc and thereafter when the Croatian forces took over Bosansko Grahovo and Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll offer into evidence 1D2774 and 1D2776.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1581 and D1582, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And both admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last area, Colonel, and that has to do with the period of time just prior to Operation Storm. I note in your statement that you left the area on 2 August 1995 prior to Operation Storm. And you note in paragraph 21 that -- and this is about second-to-last sentence -- actually second sentence you said you had discussions with Minister Susak about tactics, and in the second-to-last sentence you know any military planner would use artillery in this situation to take out the headquarters and communication centres so that any break in the line could not be reinforced. Operation Storm was an almost classic example of an offensive military operation from a tactical standpoint. As a military man talking to civilians, Colonel, can you just explain that just a little bit more in depth?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Traditionally in an offensive military operation, the offensive force would not attack across a broad front but would focus its -- its forces and penetrate through a weak part of the defence line. To ensure that its weak part, there would be an artillery preparation on military targets along the front line to -- to destroy the fighting force of the enemy and you also attack the headquarters of the military force to cause confusion and so that new orders that would redirect reinforcements could not be issued and you -- you would attack communication, military communication sites, in order to cut off their means of communicating those orders. This is typical offensive planning in the military art, and this was the planning that had I been briefed on by the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last question with regard to paragraph 22. You note that: "I do not believe that the operation" - talking about Operation Storm - "operation was designed to drive the Serbs out of Krajina. The operation was designed to re-take Croatian territory?" What's the basis of your -- or the background for that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: This was a comment that Defence Minister Susak made to me, that their objectives were to penetrate the Krajina and a move to secure the area as quickly as they could, and to minimise international criticism on -- against Croatia and to ensure that civilian or innocent personnel were not involved in the conflict. I had these same conversations with the chief of defence, General Cervenko and it was, I believe, the basis of the question that Markica Rebic, the Assistant Minister for intelligence, asked me what -- I comment in paragraph 20 what I thought or how I thought the international community would respond to an offensive operation in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of Colonel Herrick. Colonel, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. I have a small question to you: Is there any agreement between the parties about the date of the interview which was published in "Hrvatski Vojnik," because I neither see in the original nor in the translation any reference to a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you give me a moment and send an e-mail back to the office, and I think that we could find that out in short order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we wait for your answer. Mr. Cayley, any questions by the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Nothing arises from us, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions from the Markac Defence. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Herrick, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Russo. Mr. Russo is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. Colonel, I want to start off on this last topic. You indicated that had you an impression about the intent of Operation Storm and that this was based on discussions that you had had with Defence Minister Susak and also with General Cervenko and Markica Rebic, and others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And to be clear, you don't have any information about how the operation was actually conducted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know what the actual targets were for artillery fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's correct, I did not see a target list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, likewise, you don't have any information about what weaponry was used to hit what targets; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, in your witness statement at paragraph 4, you indicate that you were impressed with General Gotovina, because he was able to run a professional headquarters and was well respected by his soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I take it, then, that you viewed him as the kind of commander who could get his orders followed, if he wanted to; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: In a general sense, that's correct. There's no assurance that any commander in any army, when issuing an order, can ensure that it will be complied with, and that's why training is so critical, so that people interpret the order correctly and respond as they are trained to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. But when a commander issues an order and it's not followed, it's that commander's responsibility to take action to determine, first of all, why it wasn't followed, and, if it is not followed for some reason of insubordination, to take action; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Apologies, Colonel, just waiting for the translation. Now, at paragraph 7 of your witness statement, you state: "Because the HV lacked experienced NCOs with years of training, the NCOs that the HV did have were not able to properly instill discipline in the troops." Colonel, can you tell the Trial Chamber what it was you witnessed or heard of which made you conclude that the HV soldiers were not being properly instilled with discipline?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: And that's in paragraph 7? On the last sentence? This was a general reflection of the whole army as I looked at it. In the time that the Croatian army had to train, they were -- focussed their NCO training on the professional brigades. They did not have the means or resources or time to train the territorial force or the reserve force to the same level, and it's in that respect that I judged the army as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I do understand. What I'm looking for is if you can give the Trial Chamber something specific that you based the conclusion that there was not the proper instillment of discipline going on. Did you see something or did you hear something that led you to believe that there was some lack of discipline.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, I observed some Home Guard units in exercise. They were not as well organised or led. I didn't see any improper acts, but it was the -- the general conduct and demeanour of the soldiers when on exercise as opposed to the 4th Brigade, which I witnessed in the summer of 1994 in an exercise they conducted, so there was a clear distinction in my mind between how well the 4th Brigade operated on down in Vir and how some of the Home Guard units operated in exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to take a look at two parts of your answer. First --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, may I ask one point of clarification. I think you used the word territorial guards either in your statement or earlier in you testimony and Home Guards. Is there any distinction between the two for you or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is, and it's a lack of my specificity. The territorial guard was the -- those units of the JNA when they became under the Croatian army, the name was changed to Home Guard. But the units were essentially the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, about the Home Guard units and the observations you made about their lack of discipline, did this continue all the way up until the time-period when you left your post; that is, up until approximately late July/early August 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: It was true in the one -- in my last observation which was probably June of 1995 where I observed a Home Guard unit getting ready to go out on exercise and how they comported themselves prior to getting on to the helicopters. It was one of -- kind of a mingling around, almost like tourists, as opposed to a disciplined force that knew exactly where to position themselves and how to get on the -- the helicopter and depart the area. So I would say up until June 1995, that was still my observation of Home Guard units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you draw a distinction between the discipline excerpted by the Home Guard soldiers and that of the professional brigades, in particular the 4th Guards Brigade. However, in paragraph 11 of your statement, you state: "Even the HV professional brigades, while better, still had problems." I wonder if you could tell the Trial Chamber what were the problems that remained in the professional brigades that you were referring to here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I think in -- it was a general observation. I thought that the 4th Guards Brigade was very well disciplined. I saw them during the exercise in 1994, and then I observed a ceremony -- I want to say June 1995 in Split, and they were a very -- a military term: A very strack [phoen] unit, very disciplined and very precise in their military movements, in their use of military courtesy and the way they handle themselves. I had observed a river crossing operation earlier that spring, and while it was not done by the 4th Guards Brigade, it was conducted well but not with the precision. And it was a professional brigade, and I -- there was a composite unit so I apologise, I can't give you the exact unit. But it was not the 4th Guards. And while it was done well, it wasn't done with the same amount of precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I take it, then, that the discipline problems that you're referring to, that none of these have to do with crimes or violations of laws of armed conflict that you had no information and made not observations in those respects. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I'm referring to military operations, discipline. I have no knowledge of -- of crimes or illegal operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 13 of your witness statement, you tell the story about your encountered with a member of the 4th Guards Brigade, and you also touched on this a bit during your direct examination, I would like to ask you a couple of questions about that. I think you already told us that the location which you were going to investigate, these allegations that the HV was firing artillery at UN positions that that was in the Dinar region; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And ... and you cited this encounter with the 4th Guards Brigade soldier as an example of how, in your experience, General Gotovina's purported efforts to you to train his solders in the Laws of Armed Conflict had actually been done and was filtering down to the level of the soldier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: At least the word "had got down to the soldier," and his observation that in his military experience, in the 4th Guards Brigade, his unit had not committed these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want to make sure I'm understanding the situation correctly. This soldier who was a subordinate of General Gotovina was driving yourself and another colleague of yours to the site where you were to investigate the allegations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: We were on a mountain ridge, and we landed at a lower crest, and we were taking a jeep up to the ridge line to observe the valley, which was some distance away, so we drove part of the way by jeep and then got out and walked the rest of the way. From my vantage point, I could not conclude that the allegation was correct or incorrect, accurate or inaccurate, so I was not a part of the investigation that the UN was conducting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think you may have misunderstood my question, Mr. Herrick. I just wanted to know whether he was driving you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- to the location where this investigation was taking place.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Thank you. He was driving me up to the ridge line where I could look down into the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And he was aware, was he not, that you were a US military attache?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And this allegation was one which General Gotovina had denied; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, Colonel Herrick, did you honesty expect this soldier to tell you whether or not he had ever seen a war crime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's' fair question. No, I would not have expected him, but I did not expect him to -- to say that he his unit was proud that he had not been, and that's why it -- I remembered that particular incident. But, yes, I would have been surprised if he had said yes, we completed several war crimes and then gave me any details. That ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I'd like to show you a document regarding some of the activities of the 4th Guards Brigade a few months prior to this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could 65 ter 2271, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a report by the Bosnian SIS regarding the transport of war loot. It's dated 8 December 1994. And it reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I think it is a Herceg-Bosna Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The document reads: "Today on 7.12.1994, units of the 114th and 4th Guards Brigade are withdrawing from the Livno battlefield from the direction of Rujani-Caprazlije-Gubin-Sajkovici. 7th Guards Brigade is taking place on the front line. The units that are withdrawing from the mentioned area are taking with them the entire war loot to the Republic of Croatia. They are transporting livestock, big and small. "There is an written order on the basis of the agreement by Generals Gotovina and Blaskic regarding the transport of livestock. "Livestock is being transported to Neoric and Radosic, R. Croatia. Beside the livestock also being transport are MTS, tractors, combine harvesters, household appliance, chain-saws, et cetera, which are not part of the agreement." Now, Colonel, I take it that the 4th Guards Brigade soldier you talked to just a few months after this event failed to mention to you that his unit was taking household appliances, among other things, out of this area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's correct, he did not mention this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to admit 65 ter 2271.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2584 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, did you happen to question anyone from the 4th Guards Brigade about war crimes after their operation in Grahovo and Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You are aware, however, of what the 4th Guards Brigade, as well as other subordinates of General Gotovina, did in those towns, are you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I'm aware of allegations. I don't have specific knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I take it then that you're not a position to dispute the information that the Chamber has heard about burning and looting, which occurred in Grahovo and Glamoc by the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. I mean, if there a particular reference counsel would like to get to to show the witness, then that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness has no knowledge, apart from that there are allegations, then I take it that -- and this is how I understood Mr. Russo's question, that if he has no personal knowledge, that he is not in a position to challenge any of the allegations and, of course, at the same time, nor to confirm that, including those factual aspects of the allegations which were put before this Chamber.
