If have you anything of which you could even think of that it was before this Chamber, where you have such knowledge that you could challenge that information and we would then find out whether or not it's before this Chamber, then you are invited to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just to be clear about that, Colonel, neither General Gotovina nor Minister Susak ever discussed with you what the 4th or 7th Guards Brigade or any of the other troops under General Gotovina's command did in Grahovo and Glamoc; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, if, in fact, members of the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade and other subordinates of General Gotovina had burned residences and looted houses in that operation, that's information that you would have wanted to know about as the military attache; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Correct, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at paragraph 8 of your witness statement, you mentioned a training school established by General Gotovina, and I believe you may have also made a reference to this during your direct examination. I would like ask you if you could explain what it is you mean when you say that General Gotovina established a school. What exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: It's my understanding in talking with General Bobetko and Minister Susak and visiting the training centre at Zadar, that the -- that the school was in the operational area under the responsibility of General Gotovina and that he had played an active role in overseeing the development and training of this centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe in your direct examination you also mentioned that the leadership of the Croatian military looked to General Gotovina for the training of the NCOs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And is that what this school was supposed to do? Did General Gotovina establish this school in order to train NCOs? Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's what I was told by the senior leadership, that it was established to train NCOs of the professional brigades and that his mission was to carry that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you indicate what your understanding was of the training which was actually occurring there, and I take it that you didn't receive any information that training on the laws of armed conflict was taking place at this school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: As I state in my -- in my statement, I did not see the curriculum of the course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand that. I just want to know if perhaps someone had told you that training on the Laws of Armed Conflict was taking place at the school.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of what training was -- specific training was conducted there. And I have no knowledge that the Laws of Land Warfare were taught.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. You've given some testimony about the amount of time it takes to train non-commissioned officers properly, and you've given your opinion that that time simply was not available to the HV prior to Operation Storm. And my understanding of that, and correct me if I'm wrong, you were speaking in terms of training for operational combat tactics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's correct. Either offensive or defensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think you gave a period of several months for basic training of NCOs but that experiential training could take even years after that; is that properly understood, is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: That's correct. That's the American army experience and, to my knowledge, the experience ever other NATO countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And with respect to training on the laws of armed conflict, Colonel, how long does it take to teach troops that they shouldn't loot and burn?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, obviously the initial training would take a couple of hours, if you did it thoroughly. Hopefully you learn that as a child, that's not what you do. And then that training is continued throughout the unit training and is reinforced in every military school that you go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, I appreciate your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us about your conversation with a member of the 4th Guards Brigade who was proud that, in his unit, he had never observed any war crime being committed. How did you communicate with that person? Was that directly? I've got no idea about your knowledge of languages.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: At that time I spoke Serbo-Croatian, but my deputy was fluent in the language, and I spoke through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that conversation was with the assistance of your deputy or was it a direct or --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: It was through my deputy, but I understood the answer as the soldier said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever discuss with any of the counterparts you told us about - Mr. Gotovina, Mr. Susak - the structure and the functioning of the military justice system?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had no conversation on the military justice system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your interview is now in evidence. I'd like to ask you a few questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can give you a date on that if it would assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would certainly assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 19 November 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 19 November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I should say that is the date of the magazine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we assume that the interview was before that. I read one section of it to you. Have you recently seen it? Otherwise, we could provide you with a hard copy, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour I have not. I seen it in Croatian. I've not seen it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well -- the -- you were questioned about the cooperation between you and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. You were asked what this cooperation consists of and to what extent you were satisfied with that. Well, then, you give some explanations in relation to that. And you explain that it is important that you had direct talks with representatives of the -- of host countries and that you consider that an invaluable source of information and you are explaining that recently four US generals were visiting. Then I read to you the following four lines: "This form of cooperation is extremely useful to us in order to observe the role of the UN peace forces, in order for us to gather as much information as possible, should our army's forces assume a peacekeeping or peacemaking role in the world. Our army needs to learn more about this role." That's not entirely clear to me what the link is between observing the role of UN peace forces in order to gather information. Could you explain what you exactly wanted to say in this paragraph of the interview?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for the opportunity. We have a programme in the US Department of Defence to train newly-appointed general and flag officers. It's an -- it is to ensure that they understand US policy and defence policy. Part of their training is that they travel abroad and visit US commands and talk to foreign leaders. During this time-period, there was a group of one-star generals visiting, and I had been asked to arrange a series of discussions and meetings for them. I took that in three -- actually, there were four parts to it. They would come to the embassy and get a briefing from the US ambassador on what US policy in Croatia was. I would arrange for a working dinner with senior officers, general officers in the UN protection force that were stationed in Croatia. We would take them out to Sector West so they could talk to UN protection force personnel who were ensuring the role of the UN or the conduct of the UN operations there, and then they would have a working lunch with Defence Minister Susak, for them to talk to a senior Croatian leader on the host country's perspective of what the role of the UN was. I arranged this at the -- at the Department of Defence request, because there was some discussion on the US military taking on a greater peacekeeping role with the UN, and this was an opportunity to give new general officers firsthand impression of US policy, UN policy, and a perspective of country who was the recipient of that UN protection. And that was the reference I was making in the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that answer. In this interview, you state after you had explained that you -- that you were appointed as a military attache in the -- to the former Yugoslavia in June of 1991, prior to beginning of the war in Slovenia, that you were an "eye-witness to the beginnings of the arming of groups of people throughout Croatia." Could you tell us what kind of groups you meant and what the arming, how that took place, what you observed? Who provided the arms and to what groups?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: In my travelling through Sector West, before UN involvement and before the Vance Plan in January 1992, I travelled into Croatia, I would drive up into Hungary and then go beyond the front line and then drive back down into Croatia. And on several occasions, I would go through towns and see -- I happened to observe people handing out weapons to -- to groups of civilians or people dressed in civilian clothes. I also observed, on two occasions, JNA installations that had been taken by Croatian forces in 1992 and saw that the JNA weapons were being loaded on trucks and taken. When I asked where they were going, they said they were going to -- to be reissued to Croatian army forces. This was both small-arms and tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that was after the moment you describe in the interview, apparently, where arming of groups of people which were the beginning of the creation of defence forces of their country, that what you now describe must be later Croatian forces taking over.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, in -- I don't know who the civilian people were who were receiving weapons. Obviously the weapons that were coming out of the former JNA bases that were being reissued, the army was part of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the -- you said these weapons were given to civilians, at least to persons dressed in civilian clothes. Did you know whether these were Croats or Serbs or when you watched it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: No, sir, did I not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you link your observations very much to -- you said it was clear that ordinary people arming themselves with whatever they could get their hands were preparing for the defence of their country, their homes, their cities, those were the first units of the National Guard Corps and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. US history, too, during the War of Independence, had a difficult time early on building its defence. Then we, too, lacked organisation and a command structure." The context in which you put your observations are very much Croats, the Croatian population arming themselves in order to defend their country. At the same time, you tell me that you couldn't observe whether it were Croats or Serbs who received those weapons. Could you explain to me how the interpretation you gave to what you observed is consistent with not knowing whether it were Croats or Serbs, although it was on Croatian territory, apparently, that received those weapons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Part of that information was that my assumption that these were Croatian towns. Some towns were populated heavily by Serbs; others were populated heavily by Croats. Where I observed it was a Croatian town, though I did not stop and identify specifically who was receiving it. It was -- I believed a logical assumption on my part. It also was, I'm sure, influenced by embassy discussions, US embassy discussions I had in Zagreb with other US officers who had seen similar activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You describe in the interview, well, a type of cooperation between the United States and Croatia at the time. You said: "Finally my tasks also involved the realisation of the cooperation programme between the Croatian army and the US army." Can you tell us, to what extent was that unique for the Balkans, was that such a cooperation programme that it exists for the other republics of the former Yugoslavia as well or was it unique for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: At that time, we had no military-to-military cooperation. But the Croatian government was cooperating with the UN mandates, in terms of overflight by NATO forces, which the US was participating in, but there was no specific -- at that time, we had no US military/Croatia military relationship, formal relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I literally quoted from the interview, where you are reported to have said: "Finally" -- you were asked to explain your function as a military attache, "my tasks also involved" -- or is that -- no. "Also involved the realisation of the cooperation programme between the Croatian army and the US army." That is a literal quote, whereas your answer to my last question suggests that there was no cooperation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Well, let me be very clear, sir: There was no cooperation. I can't explain that part of the article. This may have been a misunderstanding on what the role of a military attache is. It's, generally, several parts. One is to represent the US defence department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that you mentioned four points.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I read the last one to you, which specifically refers to US/Croatian cooperation programme, even -- not even, just cooperation, but even cooperation programme. But you say that didn't exist at the time.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: No, sir, it did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in the same context, I read another few lines. You said: "I can say that we are pleased with the development of the Croatian army and are convinced that this army will be capable of defending itself and of supporting your democratic country. When full military cooperation is reached between the US and Croatia, we would like to contribute to the further development of the Croatian army in its role in protecting and defending the democratic government." This could -- the language in English is ambiguous to the extent that, if you emphasised the word "full," it suggests that there is already military cooperation; if you emphasise "cooperation," then it could be that if you say, If in the future, cooperation and full cooperation will exist, do I also have to understand this line to say that there's no cooperation at this moment but when we develop cooperation and when it has grown fully, that, under those circumstances, that the US would like to contribute to the further development of the Croatian army. Is that how I have to understand this line as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be the latter interpretation. You know, my interview was in English, it was translated into Croatian by the -- by the journalist, and it's being translated back into English again. So there may be the opportunity to interpret it several ways. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: -- the emphasise would be on the latter interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. One final question. You stated that you didn't see the curriculum at that training centre you visited. Nevertheless, you give a quite far-going assessment of the training, progress made, development of training programmes. Did you ever feel handicapped in giving such assessments by not having seen the curriculum?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I was -- I was -- the short answer is no. I was briefed by General Gotovina, I observed some training in the -- in the field, I observed the results of the training in an exercise, and there was a -- a US firm called MPRI that came to Croatia in the fall of 1994 and did a -- a full review of the curriculum and briefed me on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that then in written form?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: The briefing -- their review was in writing but the briefing was not. The briefing was oral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- who -- who -- who gave the -- or who charged MPRI with making such an assessment? Or such a review, I should say.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: MPRI was there under a US certification to provide limited training to the Croatian Ministry of Defence, and the first thing that they asked for was permission to review the current training curriculum in order to give a baseline assessment and then make recommendations on what they could offer. It was after that baseline assessment that I was briefed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you tell us who funded that -- those activities of MPRI?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: The Croatian government funded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And reported directly to the Croatian government or also to the US government?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: They reported to the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I have no further questions. Have the questions raised any need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Kehoe, and ask you how much time you would think it would take. If it's a matter of a couple of minutes, then I think that the interpreters and transcriber will be happy to stay for another couple of minutes. Is the next witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is more than a couple of minutes, and we don't have another witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have an another witness. If it is more than a couple of minutes -- would it be more than ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need to have a break first. We will have a break and we resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just a few issues that came up in the cross-examination by Mr. Russo and also some questions by Judge Orie, Colonel Herrick. The first I'd like to address is the question of follow-up, a question that Judge Orie was asking you concerning training and not seeing a curriculum. Now, how long had you been a military attache, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: When I was assigned to Zagreb, I had a military attache for about 14 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then you were there from -- your statement from 1992 to 1995. And at the time you were in Zagreb, how long had you been in the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I'd been an officer about 20 years at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now as an officer of 20 years experience, Colonel Herrick, and being a military attache in the early 1990s in Zagreb, did you draw certain conclusions merely by seeing various armies and how they moved and operated be it in exercises or just getting on to a helicopter, as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes. Over time, just by quick observation, you can make some pretty accurate judgements. It could be the care of a vehicle, are the tires new or are they worn out? Is the vehicle clean or dirty? Are the uniforms clean, are they pressed, are they maintained properly? You can tell generally by appearance a representation of how the unit operates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you say, Colonel, that how this unit looks and operates and moves together is an indication of the level of competence of that unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: It's a -- it's a representation of the training and you can assume a certain amount of competence from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I don't know whether you want to continue in this line, but it's true that I asked the witness whether he felt handicapped by not having seen the curriculum. Let's be quite clear: The curriculum was introduced -- not having seen the curriculum was introduced in chief. It's in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Russo said -- well, at least I asked questions. Now, the questions I asked were about to what extent an assessment of the training as such, as the training programmes, that's what I had in mind, is affected by not knowing the curriculum. You're now going far beyond that. You're now saying, Can you, on the basis of your experience even if you haven't seen the curriculum, can you assess the level of being trained. That was not the issue I raised and, therefore, it does not arise from my questions and if you want to put one more question I'm very generous in this respect, Mr. Kehoe, but let's not forget it has got nothing to do with my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm moving off this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, by the way, at this particular point between 1992 and 1995 were there diplomatic relations with the former Yugoslavia and the United States?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me talk to you a bit about some of the question that Mr. Russo put to, and he asked you a question: How long does it take to teach somebody not to loot, for instance, and you said, Well, just a couple of hours, something to that effect. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me just go through a few things with you based on the exhibits. And let me show you one document, 1D1604 via Sanction. By the way, I think I misspoke with regard to the last answer. Did the United States have diplomatic relations with Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I'm not -- my answer depends on -- on -- I'm not sure when they changed the formal name of the country but if we're talking about the Belgrade government, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention to the document that's on the screen which is an article on August 7th, 1995, and it is a Reuters article. If I can turn to the first paragraph. It notes that spokesman -- first paragraph: "State Department said on Monday the Croatian military has commercial consults but denied the United States provided any strategic technical or planning advice for recent Croatian military attacks. "Spokesman David Johnson said the commercial consultants operating in Croatia with a ... government licence, advise the military on how to organise democratically, maintaining civilian control, and treating civilians humanely." If we can go back down two more paragraphs where it notes that: "Johnson did not name the company by Military Professional Resource Inc. of Arlington, Virginia, has said it has a US-approved contract with Croatia to advise its military on how to operate democratically." If I can go to one other article before I ask you questions about both, and that is 1D1601, also, if we can view this by Sanction. This is a "New York Times" article from 1 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If would you just give us an opportunity to read it. Yes, there we are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as can see, this is -- date line is Croatia 29 July, and if we could go to the second page, it notes that, mid page: "In December, the State Department licenced Military Professional Resource Inc., made up of high-ranking retired military officers and based in Alexandria Virginia, to act as instructors in a course supposed to woo Croatian officers away from old Communist habits and instill the values of a democratic army." If we can go to the last paragraph, talking about comments by this individual, Ed Soyster, from MPRI. He said: "The purpose of the course was to teach Croatian officers such skills as dealing with the legislature and civilian institutions. He said that another aim of the course was to build a corps of non-commissioned officers as the backbone of the new army, which scored its important battlefield success in May when it retook areas held by Croatian Serb rebels south east of Zagreb. "We told them to expect no miracles ..." Now looking at these articles in concert and together, Colonel, if it is merely taking a few hours to instruct soldiers on the illegality of looting, why would a country like Croatia hire a company like MPRI to conduct courses, for instance, to teach the military how to treat civilians humanely, and how to have courses on developing a backbone of the new army that is non-commissioned officers. How --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't have a problem of the substance of what is being put to the witness. I do, however, have a problem with the procedure that is being followed. They're showing a document to the witness, telling him what it says, and then asking him to take it as implied in the question they're putting to him. It seems to me to be very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is extremely leading, Mr. Kehoe. What the substance of the course was is you read it now to the witness which is ... isn't it? Read that now to the witness. You should have asked the witness whether he knows what the subject of the courses was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm -- I pull it up, Mr. President, but I do believe that when the discussion concerning MPRI came up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- he did say during the course of his testimony, I believe in response to some questions by you, Your Honour, that he did know what MPRI was being hired to do. And I'm just saying, based on what he -- that substance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you then should have asked him -- if there is any place in today's transcript, and I overlook things now and then as well, where it says that -- because that's the bottom line of your question, that -- that the substance of what MPRI did was how to treat civilians humanely, then I'd like to hear where that was said. Because that is the objection by Mr. Russo, I take it. At least, of course, apart from maintaining civilian control. Is there anywhere, where the way in which civilians should be treated is mentioned as the subject of the training, advising, consulting, by MPRI to the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I not believe that it was specifically commented that -- on -- treating civilians humanely was answered, but he did note that he was familiar with the areas of instruction by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you could have asked him whether he could specify, instead of read to go him what a certain Mr. Johnson told about what is was apparently a matter which had some importance for you, because -- let's me just check. Because that was the core of your question. Why would they pay such a lot of money, to say it in other terms, to treat them and then it's something which was not yet in any way in evidence. You read it into the record so as to inform the witness to this was the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness now is at least fully aware -- I dealt with the matter in the presence of the witness, because Mr. Russo had no objections to the substance. However, I think he was right that you provided the witness with the information, where he said he had it already. You should have elicited from this witness what subjects specifically were dealt with, also that these were specifically these kind of humanitarian issues or international humanitarian law issues and then could you have asked the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back, Mr. Herrick, when we talked about your response to the question by Mr. Russo concerning taking a few hours to tell soldiers to teach them not to loot, if it is as simple as that, why would the Republic of Croatia hire a company like MPRI to conduct these courses to do, among other things, teach the military how to treat civilians humanely, and concerning developing a non-commissions corps in the Croatian military to develop the backbone of the new army. Why do they need to do that if it's as simple as saying, Don't go out there and loot?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: It's not as simple as that, and I believe I said that teaching a course on law might take a couple of hours, but it needs to be followed through in the unit by continual training, that that training is given by the non-commissioned officer corps, and the non-commissioned officer needs to be trained on the Laws of Land Warfare, and that was the -- one of the purposes of the contract between MPRI and the Croatian Ministry of Defence is to train the NCOs so that they could continue to instill that same training in their soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, in response to several questions but Mr. Russo, you were talking about the need for additional time so the NCOs could be -- could learn offensive and defensive tactics for their -- be their squads or platoons. And my question with regard to NCOs is: Within the training for a NCO, how -- how significant is the actual leadership training as it pertains to "esprit de corps" and respect for the chain of command, all of those issues, how long does those issues take and how significant are they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: For the army, leadership is absolutely critical. Leadership training in the American army is a continuing education programme from the day you enlist until the day you retire. And an American officer probably spends a third of his career in some type of formal training programme and in every one of those, a portion of that training includes leadership training, the same with our NCO corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, once again, talking about the amount of time it takes for leadership training and you talked about the lecture on what it -- how long it takes to tell someone not not to loot but what he does if he observes his troop looting. How long does that type of training take? And what he's supposed to do under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I don't have a specific time schedule for that type of training. You know, for our junior NCOs, they get a basic training as a junior enlisted person, it takes three to five years to become a junior NCO. He gets formal training on a variety of subjects from how to treat other Americans in an equal opportunity environment and the respect for individuals, that same respect for individuals is continued on in our training in the Laws of Land Warfare because the basis of how you conduct yourself with prisoners and civilians is the same. It's the respect for individual rights, and that's something that we instill in our force in -- throughout an individual's career.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Given all of these factors, Colonel, the offensive and defensive manoeuvring, the development of the "esprit de corps," all the other issues, the leadership issues that you talked about, how long would it have taken the HV, in your estimate, to train all of its NCOs on both the professional brigade level and Home Guard level. How long would that have taken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: 15 years. If it takes you 15, ten to 15 years to train a senior NCO, and he is responsible for overseeing the training and leadership of junior NCOs who are responsible for overseeing the training and leadership of enlisted -- junior enlisted men, it takes our army about 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one final area that -- concerning General Gotovina and your comment to Mr. Russo that this individual wouldn't tell you that -- had he committed crimes? Let's go to the last line of paragraph 12 -- excuse me, the last line of paragraph 13. And I'm not debating that crimes took place, sir. I want you to discuss for the Trial Chamber and clarify what you -- what you are talking about and elaborate what you were talking about concerning what General Gotovina was trying to do in that last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object to that. I don't believe that actually arises out of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It certainly does. Counsel asked the question about the 4th Guards Brigade and did he know that the 4th Guards Brigade had allegedly committed crimes in Bosansko Grahovo and other locales, and that misses the point of that particular sentence, with all due respect. The point of -- and I don't want to discuss this in front of the witness, but I will discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please, I'm afraid that the transcript it not ... I re-read the question. The questions of Mr. Russo which were a follow-up of a matter that had been raised in-chief was a further exploring whether one could expect someone to give reliable information when he says that he never observed any war crimes committed. That was the issue which was raised by Mr. Russo in cross, what went beyond what was raised in-chief. You may put questions in respect of that additional issue raised by Mr. Russo, and Mr. Russo then further gave to the witness one example of a report of what was considered to be misbehaviour. It was a HVO report referring to the 4th Guards Brigade. On that specific matter, you can put further questions to the witness, although from his answers, I took it that he no knowledge about it. Whether he has any wider knowledge of crimes committed or not being committed by the 4th Guards Brigade in the previous period is -- I wouldn't expect, in view of his earlier answers, that he would have any, but if you want to explore that, Mr. Kehoe, within those limits, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to ask a question counter to the guidance that Your Honour has just given, but given the cross-examination of counsel concerning issues that the witness obviously knew nothing about, I think that it's prudent at this point for the purposes of the Trial Chamber to ask the witness what was his point in this last sentence about the information seeping down to lower levels as in paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You explored that in examination-in-chief. You specifically dealt with this part and, therefore, we can't say that what was -- what the witness meant with that answer was something that arose in cross-examination. You dealt with it explicitly in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I liked most your first line. You said, "I don't want to ask a question counter to the guidance that Your Honour just has given." I like that one, very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I thought you would, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would invite you to follow your inclination in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Overall, Colonel, based on what you observed during this period of time, was there any doubt in your mind that General Gotovina was attempting to train his troops pursuant to the Laws of Armed Conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HERRICK
utterances.text: I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Russo, anything which came up? I would have one question. Perhaps you wait for that and see. Mr. Herrick, is the -- the training programme by -- I think it was called MPRI, is that public or is it not public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a private firm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if they have made that public or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as their programme is concerned, are you aware of their curriculum? So I'm not talking about the curriculum in the training centre that you earlier talked about, but have you any idea about the curriculum they had put in place during their training courses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a general sense, I am aware of the training that they were offering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us for a group of non-commissioned officers or for whatever group, how many hours would be spend on - and how many hours on the total - would be spent on instructions explaining that international humanitarian law is -- contains description of war crimes, so the explanation of the -- not of the -- in general violations of the laws or customs of war but violation, grave violations of the violations of the laws or customs of war. Could you tell us whether they had two days on a ten-day course on that subject; or one hour on a three-weeks' course? Could you give us an indication what percentage or what the -- what time this element would take on the totality of the course, because there seems to be a lot of other matters like detailing with the legislation and civilian authorities. I mean, that is, of course, not the kind of issues that Mr. Russo referred to, that is to train people in what is strictly forbidden because it is criminal in war. Do you have any -- could you give us an impression? If you know, if you don't remember then please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that that was a topic of the training. I cannot give you how much of the curriculum consisted of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether it was an hour or a day and on what total.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was training on the Laws of Land Warfare and there was training on how to teach the laws of land warfare but I can't give you specific times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But from your answer, I'm afraid that there is some misunderstanding of my question. The law on warfare is not specifically dealing with war crimes. Not every violation of a rule of warfare amounts to a war crime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's true, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- so, therefore, your answer is a bit confusing me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you are referring to a part of the curriculum, which is not exactly what I had in mind when I put my question to you. But perhaps my question was not clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A specific percentage of time there was -- devoted to the Laws of Land Warfare and criminal activity and the rights of individuals, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Herrick, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming a rather long way to The Hague and for answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again and my good wishes are also for Ms. Johnson and for Ms. Skibsrud. Yes, I'm looking at the wrong way. Ms. Johnson, I should have looked in your direction when I said your name; apologies for that. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom and, at the same time -- this is a public session, so, therefore, if you want to follow the proceedings, you're still welcome, but not in this special capacity anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some time left for procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I raise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- one matter. There is some confusion on the part of the Defence on the procedures for showing witnesses indirect newspaper articles, and I don't know how to bring this to the attention of the Chamber and to ask for more instruction from the Chamber on the point, so either -- do we raise it orally with the Chamber or do we do a written submission with the permission of the Chamber on the point. And it is simply a request for clarification as to what we can and can't do in light of this MPRI article. There is a specific reference that came to my mind, but I don't have time right now to find all the references, but it was with Mr. Waespi and me and Mr. Kay during Mr. Roberts' examination where a similar issue came up, and the Prosecution is allowed to put articles to the witness on the basis that the witness had communication or had -- had contacts with these two journalists, so the matters were put to him and then he was asked questions about the matters because he had contacts with the journalists. We're -- struggling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That, of course, is a situation which is quite different from the situation we had today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it was never established that this witness had anything to do with this publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But he did with MPRI and that's where we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, he gave some information in his statement and later during his testimony about MPRI, apparently an issue which was raised by Mr. Russo, which, from what I understood, was a -- well, not perhaps -- an important issue is -- in view of the total time of training, how much time would it take you to teach people that they shouldn't commit crimes. That's -- of course, it's a summary which does not pay sufficient attention to all of the details of the questions, and it had not been established at that moment that the treatment of civilians, which is, of course, in the context of this case is, at least in the Prosecution's view, not unrelated to committing crimes because civilians are a -- in international humanitarian law are persons who are persons who could be victims of crimes, and that is what has been charged in this case. Under those circumstances where the witness says that he is familiar with the MPRI training courses, then to feed him with information, what these training courses had as a substance was, in this case inappropriate, because it should -- he should have first been asked whether he could tell us what the subjects were. If he would not have known the answer, then, of course, it could have been put to him and then it might have refreshed his recollection, or he could have said, No, as far as I know, this was not part of the programme. But that's the basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's different from the earlier situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me -- my intention wasn't to argue the point on the specifics of today's session. I just -- for the record, and I would call your attention to page 6836 of the transcript, where we had, on behalf of the Defence, advanced that same argument with respect to Mr. Roberts. In other words, Mr. Kay, I believe, specifically said, We're here to hear what the witness knows and then to put matters him. Where the confusion lies, and I guess what I'm asking for is permission to request -- to file something in writing to seek specific guidance from the Chamber, is where is the line between establishing foundation through a witness that he may have knowledge about something in an article, such as establishing first that he had conversations with MPRI about their curriculum, and then putting the article to him on the basis of the foundation; or would we have been better off not establishing any foundation at all and then showing him the article and then asking him a series of questions. The -- I guess what we're trying to seek is a clarification from the Chamber because the perception -- and the perception it not always reality, and I can see that point. But the perception at this point is that it was standard practice for the Prosecution, in its direct, to put articles and newspapers and videos, et cetera, without asking first through the whole litany of foundational questions, putting it to the witness on direct, and then doing follow-up questions on the basis of both video and newspaper evidence, and my, again, perception is that our objections on the basis of leading were denied. And there may be distinctions that were missing. And in order, not only for the Gotovina Defence, as it proceeds with the rest of the case but I think for the other two Defence teams in order to know where that ground is and what procedures we need to follow to get documents in to avoid a situation where, in front of witness, we're having conversations about the proper procedure is to put articles to them, I would prefer that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me consult. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will be glad to receive brief written submissions for guidance on these matters in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One point of clarification. And my confusion was similar to my colleague's and my other colleagues on the Defence side. And my point with regard to that, given your comments, Mr. President, was not to feed the witness information. It was to counter the point raised by Mr. Russo that all you had to do was give two hours of training on this score, nothing else need be done, that there is a more complicated, which I attempted to develop and not to feed the information to the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was -- perhaps you did both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, Judge, obviously if I did both, I mean, I did both because it had been done so resolutely by my colleagues across the well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's wait what the submissions will contain. Yes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You had asked me a question earlier today. I don't know if now is a good time to raise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have reviewed our submission again and it has refreshed my memory. Of the eight documents, our understanding is that none of them were obtained through the EUMM archives. There is a question mark about two of these documents where we simply cannot not know where we received them. They were part of a larger cache of documents, electronically covering the entire region that we received in 2002 but our investigations came at a standstill. Our understanding it was collected from the region but that we could not go further to confirm that. But our understanding is that six of them for sure have not -- came from those two witness witnesses and two of those, we had in our system for at least seven years now, and they were part of a collection of hundreds perhaps even thousands of ECMM reports covering the entire former Yugoslavia, not just Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has requested to strike part of the 92 ter statement and limit the scope of testimony for Witness AG-6 who will testify on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Tuesday, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That motion is denied, but perhaps you had Witness AG-56 in mind. The reasons to follow. Another matter is where the Prosecution has urgently asked our attention for Witness AG-56 who is scheduled to testify on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe this matter has already been addressed prior to the time that the Prosecution filed for the motion, and I only received a copy of the motion while we're here in court, so I'm not able to comment much further on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also had no time to fully read it, but if I understand you well, that the Prosecution considers the 92 ter statement of Witness AG-56, a expert report where even whether he is still an expert is still to be considered, but mainly opinion and that for those reasons, it should not have been filed as a witness statement under Rule 92 ter. Is that a correct summary, Mr. Hedaraly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is partly correct, Mr. President. There were two objections which are related in some ways. The first one being as Your Honour just mentioned that our position is that he's being brought in as an expert. There are some sections of his witness statement that are clearly expert opinion and expert evidence, and we have not received the proper 30-day-time to prepare for it. Now related to this in the statement there are some documents that are referred to which are quite lengthy and are actually related to some of the opinions that he offers. For example there is a 145-page document in paragraph 3, which he uses as a support for his opinions. Now we have been told that that will not be used in direct examination because we have not received a translation for this 145-page article. So we are essentially in a situation where we cannot adequately prepare for this witness, unless the -- unless some of this expert opinion is struck down, in which case, even then, there are still some disclosure problems in terms of audio that we have not received. Two of them are an hour long. We don't have translations. We don't have transcriptions. It is just a problem now that this witness is coming in five days, and the reason that we ask that it be considered urgently is that it looks like we won't be sitting tomorrow. We have a witness on Monday, and by then, it may be too late for us to prepare. Our position would be that if he will testify as to what is in his statement, we will need more time to prepare and receive complete disclosures of what is contain in the statement and translations of those, and if those portions are struck down and he testifies as a fact witness under Rule 92 ter, then obviously we will need the remaining disclosures as soon as possible so that we can effectively prepare for his testimony on Tuesday, otherwise we will be in a position to ask that his testimony be postponed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object, first of all, because this is being raised at quarter to 7.00 on a Thursday. The statement itself was disclosed, I believe, late May /early June at the latest. Well, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then the first thing to try to find --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a common position on when it was disclosed. I can only say that I saw it this morning for the first time, but that's, of course, is a totally different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that quite frankly I haven't even read their motion yet, so there is no reason why this shouldn't have been brought to my attention before, and if it is now urgent and last-minute for the Prosecution, it is because they raised it at the last minute, and I shouldn't have to prepare a response now orally to something that's been filed in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm mainly raising the issue because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, B/C/S was given to Prosecution on 20th of May and the English translation on 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the 30-day issue really they have -- they will have had it certainly more and in 30 days, if it was an issue with respect to Rule 94 and whether it should be also filed under Rule 94, that also could have been brought to our attention weeks ago. To now tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whatever the case is, the Chamber, as I said before, has received this morning the filing of the 92 ter statement. The Chamber has now looked at the Prosecution's response. I'm not saying read the Prosecution's response, but has looked at it. And whatever the case is from reading the -- what is offered as a 92 ter statement. For the Chamber, we have at least to determine how urgent the matter is. So, therefore, for us, it has a certain urgency. Even if we decide it is not urgent, that decision is in view of the time-frame, is a decision which urgently should be taken. Therefore, that's the main reason, and because we're not sitting tomorrow, why I raised the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in brief, what we would reply to that is that -- this is now again -- if you have taken a look at it, I haven't even had one eye on it yet -- is essentially the Leslie standard which was established very earlier on in this case, so it's not being offered as expert testimony; however, he does have opinion opinions on the matter. Whether he is qualified to give them or not, I am perfectly happy if the Chamber wishes to proceed that way with establishing a foundation in his background and educational background and publications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's a lot of background, I would say. In the 92 ter statement there is a background experience, academic experience to such an extent that when I read it, and I have not properly looked at the motion, I thought as a matter of fact that I was reading an expert report. That's -- I'm quite frank that might be because I should have read better. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The reality is that the background is there because of the issues in 1996 that have been raised by the Prosecution and the witness is a fact witness with respect to return of refugees to the area because he was the person in charge by the Croatian government to coordinate the return of both Croat and Serb refugee to the area. His demographic background then is his education, his understanding of the issue, et cetera, goes towards certainly his knowledge of what he was doing in 1996 and to the extent he has opinions that are related to that, again, based on the Leslie --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what you're facing is, as a matter of fact, the balance between fact and opinion. From the decision, I just -- although reasons not being there yet. The decision in relation to Witness AG-6, it may appear that this witness is not overly strict in saying whenever there comes an opinion, it's not anymore for a witness to tell us about, but I think the issue most likely will be here, whether we are now at the other side of the -- of the -- of the scale -- not of the scale but the other side of the range. Is it witness testimony where some opinions have slipped in and that's what happens and that's sometimes accepted and to a certain degree accepted, or is it primarily opinion. I think this seems to be the issue and this, of course, may have consequences for how to prepare for cross-examination for such a witness or such an expert. The reason why I'm raising it is because it would be -- if the motion would be denied, then, of course, we would hear the testimony of the witness on Tuesday. If, however, the motion would be granted, then, of course, we have a very practical problem, that is, how to use our court time as good as possible. I fully accept that you had no -- not a lot of time to read all this, so I'm trying to find out whether there's any way to communicate tomorrow in such a way and, of course, we could schedule a court hearing, but that might not be the best way to do it, but in order to see how the Chamber receives a further input from the Defence and perhaps a further response from the Prosecution so as to at least make up its mind under which direction the decision would go. That's the reason why I'm raising the matter. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The -- thank you, Mr. President. I'm know we don't have time. I'm not going to respond to everything Mr. Misetic has said. I simply want to point out there's also the disclosure issue so that if the Chamber ultimately decides that this witness can testify as to his opinions contained in the statement that is based in large part on some documents that we have not received translations for. So I just want to -- I know the Chamber has considered it, but I just want to -- that we don't forget the second issue as well, which is directly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My main point is that whatever the decision would be to grant the motion -- to grant the motion filed by the Defence and declare that -- come to the conclusion that you are -- the objection you've raised are not of a kind to -- to not accept the newer statement or whether it would be the other way around or whether we would say the urgency is not there, you should have raised it at any earlier stage. Normally a 92 ter decision is taken when the witness appears. Now, that seems to be, under the present circumstances, not something we should just wait for and see what happens on Tuesday. Because if the Chamber would decide that either disclosure was done in a way which has given insufficient opportunities for preparation, under those circumstances, we would have nothing. So, therefore, the Chamber is inclined to see whether it can make up its mind at an earlier stage, so as to fill a possible gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just respond, Mr. President. It's my understanding we're talking about four exhibits. This is not by any stretch of the imagination of any significant prejudice to the Prosecution. Let me note that with Mr. Theunens, for example, it was, I believe, close to 15 exhibits that we didn't receive until five days before he began to testify. If I'm not mistaken, we're five days out right now. At some point, the realities of trial and the strains on our translators have to be taken into consideration, which I alerted to -- the Prosecution to before we came to court today. So I'm reasonably confident that they will have these four documents tomorrow by the close of business. The audios. They're not audios; they're videos. The entire videos have been disclosed to the Prosecution on May 4th. What they're looking for is a selection, but the disclosures themselves have happened. I would again point out that we are doing nothing that hasn't been done by the Prosecution in its direct. As a matter of fact, Mr. President, our standard is to hold ourselves at least to what the Prosecution did and held itself in its case in-chief and hopefully to do a little bit better, and that's what we're trying to do. So, to that extent, Mr. President, I can assure you they will have the material by the close of business tomorrow. With respect to Your Honour's instruction to me, is it that you wish that I file a reply by tomorrow or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to achieve is that the Chamber receives all the relevant information to see whether there's a fair chance that we would hear the testimony of this witness on Tuesday, or not, and not to leave that until Friday -- until Tuesday morning, because then we might have difficulties in filling the gap. Now, another matter is that, if the Chamber would decide that the Prosecution would need more time, would there be any way of filling the gap?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is no way to fill the gap, firstly. Second - and this is another practical matter for the Chamber to consider - without getting into the details, the witness needs to travel by car, and so I'm pretty sure he is set to leave on Saturday so that he can be ready to go on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is another reason why we should not leave the matter until Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be a practical solution if -- first of all, that the parties try to resolve some of the matters, such as incomplete disclosure, that -- or selection of certain portions of a video, that you communicate in such a way that we see how big the problems really are. That is the disclosure issue. And that, for example, that tomorrow, at noon, or tomorrow at 2.00 p.m., there would be informal communication with the Chamber, either through e-mail, or, if need be, by a meeting to just establish where we stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me state this. I'm now advised that we have four documents outstanding and the video-clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, I was just about to see whether you read the response that you haven't read yet. You tell Mr. Hedaraly exactly what is missing, and then he can say, You're wrong because that and that is missing as well. This is it not -- you say it's very limited. And then that tomorrow there would be a point in time, whether there will be a communication, and, of course, it depends a bit on what the parties can achieve, what type of communication that should be, that could be -- meeting on practical matters. It could be an exchange of a common position by e-mail. It could be anything. But that we further communicate tomorrow how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Your Honour, and we will do that in morning. What I wanted to do was correct the record, though, so that -- I had misspoken before because I was unaware that actually CLSS is doing two of the documents, and they will be ready on Monday, according to CLSS. Two of the documents will be translated by us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber expects you to further communicate. And would noon be a right time, 2.00 p.m. be the right time, to make an inventory of where we are?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Since we have no court tomorrow, I'm sure we can meet in the morning, and by 12.00 or 1.00, I'm sure that we can get back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe likes to sleep in, but I think we can get it done by noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We can have that redacted, Mr. President. We have no objection to that being redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's good that this is the last day of the week in which we are sitting. There will be communication tomorrow not later than by 1.00. The parties will be informed who will be in charge in Chambers staff, and the parties should remain stand by to further meet, if need be, to see whether we can resolve this matter. We resume on Monday, the 13th of July, at 9.00, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of July, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
